A lot of the criticism I see here is along the lines of "What, a person isn't allowed to change their opinion on something?" I propose there are two important distinctions to be made in this situation:

  1. Nothing substantial about the issue (set aside public approval) has changed. Seriously, this was a large part of the right's argument when the case was brought to the Supreme Court. In the opinion of this humble poster, anyone who is not influenced by some sort of bias can see how backwards and nonsensical such a position is. I agree politicians are human, and to err is human, BUT:

  2. As a PRESIDENTIAL CANDIDATE, we should have huge expectations. We aren't talking about your cousin who recently moved out of a rural Mississippi area and has discovered "the gays" aren't trying to take over the world. We are talking about someone who has been influencing and has been exposed to a huge variety of political decisions for decades. This person is applying for one of the most powerful positions on Earth.

It is this voater's belief that such a person must be a forward-thinking individual. He or she should be able to see beyond the horizon, have a vision, and be able to execute it. If a candidate doesn't have that foresight, I question how he or she would be able to effectively make decisions to prepare us for the future. It's been reasonably obvious for a long time (at least to me, and I know I'm not alone) that "gay rights" was coming. This means at least one of the following is true:

 

a) Hillary was unable to predict this would happen

b) Hillary adopted or changed her official position for political reasons

c) Hillary allowed a bias to influence her professional position

 

Suffice to say, none of the above options are a desirable quality for a presidential candidate
